localBiteReport: Reports from the past week out of Choctawhatchee Bay and Santa Rosa Beach show speckled trout as the standout inshore species, with guides describing good numbers and quality fish being caught across the bay. A charter out of Santa Rosa Beach reported a bull redfish over 40 inches and 26 lbs landed just days ago, and other charters have been putting clients on flounder and slot redfish as well. Water temps are sitting at 85°F, and the summer pattern has trout and reds most active early morning and late evening on the flats, pulling tighter to deeper docks and shaded structure during midday heat. Wind has been a factor in recent weeks, requiring guides to be selective about where they fish, but overall the inshore bite is described as solid. The most recent Half Hitch Destin report is dated 7-13-26 but full inshore details were not accessible; their most recently readable bay content points to nighttime trout fishing on live shrimp and topwater redfish action on the flats as the go-to summer patterns.

aiSummary: Speckled trout are the standout species across Choctawhatchee Bay right now, with guides reporting good numbers and quality fish, plus slot redfish, flounder, and even a 40-inch-plus bull red landed near Santa Rosa Beach this past week. Water temps are sitting at 85°F and the summer pattern puts trout and reds most active in the early morning and late evening hours, with fish pulling tight to deeper, shaded structure through the midday heat. A 24% storm chance arrives before 1 PM today, so plan to be off open water or tucked into protected bayous well before then.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay and acts as a current funnel, pushing bait through on both tides and concentrating trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum around the pilings year-round. The lee-side pilings are the prime ambush zone on an incoming tide, as fish stack up waiting for bait to sweep past. Being open water at a bay chokepoint, it's the first spot to become uncomfortable or unfishable when wind and chop build.
bridge.todaysCall: The tide is falling hard through the afternoon with low water at 3:27 PM, so the current funnel at the bridge will be moving bait aggressively through the pilings — get there early and fish the outgoing flow before the storm window opens before 1 PM. Light westerly winds at 5–10 mph will create some chop on the open water approach, so keep an eye on conditions and don't linger once the sky starts building. With a near-full waxing gibbous moon pushing strong spring tides, current through the bridge should be pronounced, which historically lights up trout and redfish on the structure. Slightly stained water gives fish a slight edge, so lean toward darker soft plastics or live shrimp tight to the pilings. Plan to be off this exposed water well before noon given the storm risk.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers some of the most protected inshore water on the bay, with a strong year-round redfish population and trout and flounder showing at the creek mouth around the oyster bars. Tree cover keeps the upper bayou a few degrees cooler than open bay water and provides a reliable refuge from wind and building weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish and can hold bass alongside smaller reds.
alaqua.todaysCall: Today's combination of 85°F water, summer heat, and a storm window before 1 PM makes Alaqua's shaded, protected water an excellent choice — the tree canopy will provide some relief from the 93°F heat and the spot stays fishable in nearly any weather. Hit the oyster bars at the mouth early on the falling tide to intercept trout and reds as bait moves out; the near-full moon is driving strong tidal movement, so that transition should be active. Slightly stained water suits redfish well here — weedless gold spoons or live shrimp on a popping cork along the grass edges are reliable summer producers. If the bay-wide trout bite is any indication, the creek mouth should hold fish through the early morning before the heat pushes them deeper into shade. Be back at the ramp or deep inside the creek before the storm risk window peaks.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees lighter fishing pressure than nearby Alaqua and LaGrange, meaning the fish here tend to be less educated and more willing to bite. The interior grass flats are prime sight-fishing territory for redfish in water under two feet, and pompano occasionally work the mouth on moving tides. It is somewhat less sheltered than LaGrange when weather builds from the south or west.
basin.todaysCall: Lighter pressure and willing reds on the interior grass flats make Basin Bayou worth an early morning visit today, but keep the 24% storm chance before 1 PM in mind — the bayou offers moderate protection, so don't push your luck on the flats when clouds start stacking. The falling tide through the morning will concentrate reds and trout along grass edges and the bayou mouth; the strong spring tide from the near-full moon will push that movement aggressively. Slightly stained water makes a subtle gold spoon or a live shrimp under a float a smart pick for the flats. Get your sight-fishing done in the low-angle morning light before the sun climbs and the heat index approaches 105°F, then consider transitioning to deeper structure or heading in ahead of the afternoon storm window.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is consistently the top trout producer in this part of the bay, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth, interior grass flats loaded with redfish year-round, and deep interior holes that hold black drum and sheepshead. It is also the most weather-protected water on the western side of the bay, making it the default choice when conditions deteriorate. The combination of structure variety and reliable protection makes it a go-to for guides when they need to put fish in the boat.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange is a strong pick for today — it offers the best storm protection on this side of the bay, which matters given the pre-1 PM storm window, and the summer trout bite has been exceptional bay-wide. Fish the iconic oyster bars at the mouth early on the outgoing tide, which will be running with force thanks to the near-full moon spring tide; trout and reds should stack on the upcurrent edge of the bars as bait pours out. Slightly stained water rewards anglers who slow down and fish live shrimp or natural-colored soft plastics close to structure. As the morning heats up toward 93°F and a heat index of 105°F, shift focus to the deep interior holes where black drum and sheepshead hold in cooler water through midday. You can stay here safely even if weather builds — just keep watching the sky and be ready to sit tight inside the bayou if needed.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a short tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the open bay, making it the most convenient and fastest-access fishery on the dashboard. Incoming tides push baitfish up into the bends and grass edges, concentrating redfish and trout, while the creek mouth is a reliable flounder zone. The upper section transitions to brackish water and can hold bass alongside smaller reds. Its compact, protected nature makes it the safest option when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: With a storm chance before 1 PM and heat index topping 105°F today, Four Mile Creek's proximity to Shipyard Marina and its protected character make it a smart, low-risk option — you're never far from the dock. The tide is outgoing through the morning toward a 3:27 PM low, so focus on the creek mouth and lower bends where bait is funneling out; the strong spring tide from the near-full moon will push that flow hard, which tends to activate trout and reds in the tighter bends. Flounder have been showing in recent bay-wide reports, and the creek mouth is a prime zone to work a slow bottom-bouncing rig or paddle tail on the tide change. Slightly stained water means fish are hunting by vibration and scent as much as sight — a live or fresh-dead shrimp on the bottom is hard to beat here. Keep your timeline short and be back at the marina with buffer time before the storm window.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide destination and one of the most productive trout flats on all of Choctawhatchee Bay. Summer mornings are peak season, with trout stacked on grass in two to four feet of water, and Spanish mackerel push into the mouth on moving tides. It sees regular guide pressure but continues to produce consistently, and its distance from the 331 Bridge area means factoring in run time from Shipyard Marina.
hogtown.todaysCall: Bay-wide reports specifically call out the Santa Rosa Beach area as producing excellent speckled trout right now, and Hogtown Bayou is the signature flat for that pattern — an early start here today could be very rewarding. The near-full moon is driving strong spring tides, and the falling tide through the morning will move bait across the grass flats in 2–4 feet, which is exactly the depth trout stack in during summer. Get on the water at or before sunrise (5:58 AM) to maximize the low-light feeding window before the 93°F heat pushes fish off the flats to deeper, cooler water. Slightly stained water and a light W wind at 5–10 mph are workable conditions; live shrimp under a popping cork or a slow-sinking twitchbait are proven summer trout producers here. Factor in the longer run time from the marina and commit to being off the open flats and heading back well before the storm window opens before 1 PM.

rocky.aiNote: Rocky Bayou sits inside Fred Gannon Rocky Bayou State Park near Niceville, offering a scenic, significantly less pressured fishery far from the crowds near the 331 Bridge. Freshwater influence from Rocky Creek makes it an excellent flounder destination, and the glass-calm state park coves are ideal for sight-fishing redfish. Mangrove snapper hold around dock pilings throughout the warmer months, and the protected park setting keeps conditions calm even when the open bay is choppy. It is the farthest location from Shipyard Marina, so run time must be factored into trip planning.
rocky.todaysCall: Rocky Bayou's distance from the marina is the biggest logistical consideration on a day with a pre-1 PM storm window — build in extra margin so you're not caught in open water on the run back if afternoon cells fire early. That said, the calm, protected state park water and low pressure make it worth the trip if you can launch early; light W wind at 5–10 mph and slightly stained water are comfortable conditions for the sight-fishing the coves are known for. Work the grass edges and coves for redfish on the falling tide, and probe dock pilings for mangrove snapper with small live shrimp or cut bait — both patterns suit today's warm 85°F water well. Flounder have been appearing in recent bay-wide reports, and Rocky Creek's freshwater influence makes the bayou's lower reaches a prime target for flatfish on a slow bottom presentation. Leave the water by 11:30 AM at the latest to ensure a safe run home ahead of the storm window.
